quizzes.title: Legal framework: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage:
The Mahanadi dispute between Odisha and Chhattisgarh concerns how the river's water is shared, especially in the non-monsoon season, when water flowing downstream becomes critically important. The absence of a formal inter-state water-sharing agreement has added to the conflict, and Odisha has argued that upstream construction in Chhattisgarh has reduced the flow reaching its own territory. Chhattisgarh, for its part, maintains that it has a legitimate right to use river waters and that its projects serve regional development.

Such disputes are handled through a separate arrangement. The Constitution provides for them, and the law built on it allows a tribunal to be set up when a dispute needs adjudication. The tribunal then issues its decision, and the matter is decided on the basis of available evidence and legal principles.

The Mahanadi tribunal has expressed concern about repeated adjournments and the lack of substantive progress in talks. It has observed that no concrete proposals have been placed on record, despite assurances of settlement efforts. The tribunal has therefore given both states a final opportunity to agree on a formula.

Other river disputes in the country have also been handled through tribunals, each set up for a particular river. Read together, these cases show that water sharing between states is governed by a special framework rather than by routine legal channels.

questions.q: When a state approaches the Centre seeking a tribunal, what does the Centre first do?
options: Refers the matter to the Supreme Court
Transfers the dispute to a River Board
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Centre first tries consultation among the aggrieved states and constitutes a tribunal only if that fails.

questions.q: How often must a River Board meet under the River Boards Act, 1956?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that a River Board is to meet at least thrice a year.

questions.q: Entry 56 of which list empowers the Union to regulate and develop inter-state rivers in public interest?
questions.explanation: Entry 56 is placed in the Union List, which gives the Union this power.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court cannot question the award or formula given by an inter-state water tribunal.
Reason (R): The Supreme Court can question the working of such a tribunal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but R describes what the court can examine and does not explain why it cannot question the award.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Article 262   ->   A. Parliament adjudicates disputes relating to inter-state rivers
II. River Boards Act, 1956   ->   B. Boards for inter-state rivers set up in consultation with states
III. Entry 17 (State List)   ->   C. Water supplies, irrigation, canals, drainage and embankments
IV. Entry 56 (Union List)   ->   D. Regulation and development of inter-state rivers in public interest
questions.explanation: Each provision matches its description in the booklet, with Article 262 linked to adjudication by Parliament.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Entry 17 of the State List covers irrigation and drainage.
II. Article 262 allows Parliament to exclude courts' jurisdiction in inter-state river disputes.
III. The Supreme Court may set aside the award of a tribunal.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II match the booklet, while III contradicts the booklet's position that the Supreme Court cannot question an award.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A River Board must meet at least thrice a year.
II. Entry 56 lies in the State List.
III. Consultation among aggrieved states comes before a tribunal is constituted.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct, while II is wrong because Entry 56 is in the Union List.

questions.q: Under which entry of the Union List can the Union regulate and develop inter-state rivers in public interest? (number)

questions.q: Under which entry of the State List do states get powers over water supplies and irrigation? (number)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of times per year that a River Board must meet? (numeral)

questions.q: What does the Centre first try among aggrieved states before constituting a tribunal? (one word)

questions.q: In which year was the River Boards Act enacted? (four digits)
questions.explanation: The River Boards Act was passed in 1956, the same year as the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act.

questions.q: According to the booklet, the Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award or formula but can question its ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court can question the working of a tribunal but not its award or formula.

quizzes.title: River course: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage:
The Mahanadi is at the centre of a long-running dispute because its water supports many activities along its course. Downstream areas rely on the river for irrigation, drinking water, fisheries and the wider ecology of the area. When flow declines, these uses come under strain, and the concern becomes most acute during the non-monsoon season.

The river is fed by a network of tributaries that join it along its length. Its waters therefore reflect conditions across a large catchment, and activities in upstream areas can affect what reaches the lower reaches. Upstream construction is one such activity, and it has been cited as a reason for falling downstream flow. Water reaching any point along the river thus depends on conditions upstream.

Large infrastructure also lies on the river. Among these works is a dam that has been a major point of attention in discussions of the river. The presence of such structures makes it harder to assess the river's flow without reliable information. Such works are discussed in relation to the river's flow and its sharing among states.

The booklet includes a map of the river, which helps readers follow its path through the region. Its course is described in a short section that covers the river's main features. The booklet's summary is brief, so the map and text together give a basic picture of the river.

questions.q: Where does the Mahanadi originate?
questions.explanation: The booklet places the origin of the Mahanadi at Sihawa Hill in Raipur, Chhattisgarh.

questions.q: Into which water body does the Mahanadi finally empty?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Mahanadi flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: Which set of tributaries joins the Mahanadi from its right bank?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists Jonk, Ong and Tel as the right bank tributaries.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Mahanadi originates in Odisha.
Reason (R): The river flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: A is false because the origin is Sihawa Hill in Chhattisgarh, while R is true as the booklet says the river flows through Odisha.

questions.q: Which left-bank tributary of the Mahanadi is listed last?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists the left bank tributaries as Shivnath, Hasdeo, Mand and Ib, with Ib last.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Tel is a right bank tributary of the Mahanadi.
II. Mand is a right bank tributary of the Mahanadi.
III. The Mahanadi empties into the Arabian Sea.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement I is correct, since Mand is a left bank tributary and the river empties into the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Ib is a left bank tributary of the Mahanadi.
II. Jonk is a left bank tributary of the Mahanadi.
III. The river empties into the Gulf of Kutch.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement I is correct, since Jonk is a right bank tributary and the river empties into the Bay of Bengal.

quizzes.title: Other tribunals: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage:
India has several inter-state water tribunals, and each one has been set up for a particular river dispute. The booklet lists tribunals formed at different points over the years, and each entry links a tribunal to the states involved in that dispute. Several states appear in more than one tribunal, so disputes over different rivers can involve the same state.

The Mahanadi tribunal is one of the bodies in the table. It was set up to resolve the sharing of the Mahanadi's waters between the two states along the river. The tribunal has been dissatisfied with repeated adjournments and a lack of progress, and it has granted both states a final opportunity to reach a formula.

The booklet presents the tribunals in a table with three columns: the name of each tribunal, its year of formation, and the states involved. The table covers five tribunals in total. Each entry records the name, the year and the states, so the table gives a compact summary of the disputes it covers.

Taken together, these entries show that India has used separate tribunals for separate rivers, each tied to its own set of states. The table is part of a wider discussion in the booklet about inter-state river disputes and the legal framework for resolving them.

questions.q: In which year was the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II formed?
questions.explanation: The booklet's table lists the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II as formed in 2004.

questions.q: How many states are involved in the Ravi & Beas Water Tribunal?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists three states for the Ravi & Beas Water Tribunal: Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab.

questions.q: Which tribunal includes Telangana among the states involved?
questions.explanation: The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II covers Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Karnataka.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Karnataka is a party to the Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal.
Reason (R): Karnataka is one of the states in the Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: A is false because the Vansadhara tribunal covers Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, while R is true because Karnataka is in the Mahadayi tribunal.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Ravi & Beas Water Tribunal   ->   A. Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab
II. Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal   ->   B. Karnataka, Goa and Maharashtra
III. Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal   ->   C. Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
IV. Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II   ->   D. Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Karnataka
questions.explanation: Each tribunal in the booklet's table is matched with its listed states in the last option.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal was formed in 2010.
II. The Ravi & Beas Water Tribunal involves Punjab.
III. The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II involves Odisha.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II match the table, while III is wrong because Odisha is not in the Krishna tribunal.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal was formed in 2010.
II. The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal II involves four states.
III. The Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal involves Punjab.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while III is wrong because the Mahanadi tribunal covers Chhattisgarh and Odisha.
